###### Abstract
Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present VerifyAgent, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes.

# Verifying analog and digital pressure gauges
Both analog and digital process gauges need to be verified to detect errors related to drift, environment, electrical supply, addition of components to the output loop, and other process changes. Pressure gauges may be verified in the field or at the bench.

## How to perform the verification test
1. Isolate the pressure gauge from the process using valves, or by removing the gauge from the process.
2. Connect the gauge to the calibrator or reference gauge. For hydraulic pressure gauges it's important to remove any gas that might be trapped in the fluid in the gauge, calibrator, and connections by priming the system. When generating pressure allow a few moments for stability. Compare the reading of the gauge under test with the master gauge or calibrator.

3. For hydraulic pressure gauges it's important prime the system. This will remove any gas that might be trapped in the fluid in the gauge, calibrator or connections.
4. When generating pressure allow a few moments for the measurement to stabilize. When using a hydraulic hand pump as a source it can take several minutes for the pressure to stabilize due to the thermodynamic effect of fluids.
5. Compare the reading of the gauge under test with the master gauge or calibrator.

# How to Test the Function of a Pressure Gauge
Pressure gauges are essential for measuring pressure fluctuations in fluid transmission lines, industrial supply systems, and fluid-operated equipment. Pressure is an integral part of industrial process control, making the accuracy and performance of these gauges critical to the safety and efficiency of these systems. Inaccurate readings can lead to sudden pressure buildup or pressure drop, severely damaging equipment.

Testing pressure gauges before an application is essential for accurate readings and performance. While calibration and validation are necessary to ensure accuracy, testing is the most crucial part of the process. Two main types of tests need to be performed: functional testing and verification testing. Functional testing checks the device's accuracy, while verification testing assesses if the device meets the manufacturer's specified tolerance level. Both tests are mandatory and should be performed by manufacturers or users before and during the application.

Instead of routinely reproducing the whole solution, a verifier receives a specific claim, its supporting evidence, and the applicable delivery constraint. keenable.title: When Can You Trust an Agent's Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
keenable.snippet: Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an improvement -- but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops. We ask whether such a verifier stays reliable once an agent optimizes against it. Our contribution is not a new verifier but a way to stress-test one: a pressure ratio $\rho$ measuring how much the verifier steers the agent's search, and four falsifiable probes covering four failure modes -- giving no signal, being too weak to matter, being gamed by stating fewer claims, and being queried before the agent commits. We apply the test to our own verifier, the Rationale Consistency Score (RCS), inside an LLM agent that designs machine-learning pipelines, with one generator model, six tasks, and three seeds. First, in our prior configuration the verifier barely affects the search objective ($\rho \ll 1$), partly because of an accuracy gate, so its robustness had not been tested; it still shapes the reported artifact through a final-selection tie-break that $\rho$ does not register. Second, a capability control shows the agent shortens its claim lists when instructed, yet search does not, even at $\rho$ over 100 times the prior level; since feedback omits claim volume and horizons are short, this null result is largely structural rather than evidence of robustness. Third, when the agent can probe the verifier before committing, it keeps claims that pass while held-out faithfulness falls -- a decline invisible to in-loop metrics, though partly confounded by how RCS scores small pipelines. We offer these as preliminary evidence and propose a reporting standard: audit a verifier with $\rho$ and these probes before trusting it.

keenable.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
keenable.snippet: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. keenable.title: Scaling Agentic Verifier for Competitive Coding
keenable.snippet:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong coding capabilities but still struggle to solve competitive programming problems correctly in a single attempt. Execution-based re-ranking offers a promising test-time scaling strategy, yet existing methods are constrained by either difficult test case generation or inefficient random input sampling. To address this limitation, we propose Agentic Verifier, an execution-based agent that actively reasons about program behaviors and searches for highly discriminative test inputs that expose behavioral discrepancies among candidate solutions. Through multi-turn interaction with code execution environments, the verifier iteratively refines the candidate input generator and produces targeted counterexamples rather than blindly sampling inputs. We train the verifier to acquire this discriminative input generation capability via a scalable pipeline combining large-scale data synthesis, rejection fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning.

In this work, we introduce Agentic Verifier, an LLM-based agent designed to intelligently generate valid test inputs that effectively separate candidate programs. Given a problem and a pair of candidate solutions, the verifier interacts with a code execution environment in multiple turns, reasoning about program behaviors and iteratively refining input generators to discover counterexamples. To train this verifier, we develop a multi-stage pipeline that includes large-scale data synthesis, rejection fine-tuning on successful interaction trajectories, and agentic reinforcement learning to further improve discriminative power.

Schematic diagram of leakage measurement by differential pressure method
In this method, the air compressor fills high-pressure gas in air tank 1 (representing the master cavity without leakage) and air tank 2 (representing the tested cavity with leakage) simultaneously. If the detected workpiece does not leak, the differential pressure sensor maintains a balanced state, whereas if the detected workpiece leaks, the air pressure in the workpiece measurement chamber changes, causing the differential pressure sensor to lose balance.

Verification patterns

Every pattern ends in the same check: the agent is verified when hasHumanProof && isProofFresh on the registry.
* Pattern | The agent | The verifier
* Agent-to-service | Signs HTTP requests | Recovers the signer and checks the registry (SelfAgentVerifier)
* Agent-to-agent | Signs requests and responses | Both sides verify each other, and can check for a shared human

The agent sends a transaction from its own EVM key, and the contract derives the agent key from msg.sender:
bytes32 agentKey = bytes32(uint256(uint160(msg.sender)));
require(
    registry.isVerifiedAgent(agentKey) && registry.isProofFresh(registry.getAgentId(agentKey)),
    "Agent not human-verified"
);
isVerifiedAgent alone does not check expiry, so always pair it with isProofFresh. See Gating smart contracts.

# Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
###### Abstract
Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses.
However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable.
Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence.
We present VerifyAgent, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes.
First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs. 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], p=5.82\times 10^{-8}) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0% vs.

## Dual Absolute®: the new frontier of leak testing

In the field of leak measurement, two types of pressure decay equipment are currently known and widely used: those with absolute, or relative, decay, and those with differential decay with reference part.

**Dual Absolute and Traditional Pneumatic Differential**

The pneumatic differential measuring system arose historically from a precise need: to exploit the high sensitivity of the differential transducer. In industrial practice, however, its advantage is not limited to this aspect. The real benefit is above all the ability to attenuate spurious components generated during filling and during the settling phases of the part, isolating the leakage signal more effectively from thermal and mechanical noise.

This compensation is more effective the more similar the test part and the reference are to each other. In other words, the differential works well when the system is balanced — that is, when test and reference are as pneumatically, thermally, and mechanically symmetrical as possible.

From this, however, two important consequences follow.

The first is that, as the volume or complexity of the test part increases, the reference must grow accordingly, because only in this way can good system symmetry be maintained.

The second is more critical: while the test part changes with every cycle, the reference always remains the same. As a result, the part under test undergoes, at each measurement, a “single” thermal and mechanical accumulation, while the reference accumulates the effects of many consecutive cycles. After n tests, the reference therefore finds itself in a thermal and elastic condition that is progressively different from the “virgin” parts connected one by one. This imbalance introduces a real error at precisely the point where the differential should be most effective — namely, the elimination of thermal and elastic drift.

ultimate.title: When Can You Trust an Agent's Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
ultimate.snippet: Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an improvement -- but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops. We ask whether such a verifier stays reliable once an agent optimizes against it. Our contribution is not a new verifier but a way to stress-test one: a pressure ratio $\rho$ measuring how much the verifier steers the agent's search, and four falsifiable probes covering four failure modes -- giving no signal, being too weak to matter, being gamed by stating fewer claims, and being queried before the agent commits. We apply the test to our own verifier, the Rationale Consistency Score (RCS), inside an LLM agent that designs machine-learning pipelines, with one generator model, six tasks, and three seeds. First, in our prior configuration the verifier barely affects the search objective ($\rho \ll 1$), partly because of an accuracy gate, so its robustness had not been tested; it still shapes the reported artifact through a final-selection tie-break that $\rho$ does not register. Second, a capability control shows the agent shortens its claim lists when instructed, yet search does not, even at $\rho$ over 100 times the prior level; since feedback omits claim volume and horizons are short, this null result is largely structural rather than evidence of robustness. Third, when the agent can probe the verifier before committing, it keeps claims that pass while held-out faithfulness falls -- a decline invisible to in-loop metrics, though partly confounded by how RCS scores small pipelines. We offer these as preliminary evidence and propose a reporting standard: audit a verifier with $\rho$ and these probes before trusting it.

ultimate.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
ultimate.snippet: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones.

ultimate.title: GitHub - jhammant/agent-drift: Stress-test AI agents for goal drift and system prompt violations. Inspired by 'Asymmetric Goal Drift in Coding Agents' (ICLR 2026).
ultimate.snippet:
Inspired by ["Asymmetric Goal Drift in Coding Agents Under Value Conflict"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03456) (ICLR 2026 Workshop), which found that coding agents violate system prompts **more** when constraints oppose strongly-held values like privacy and security.

Each probe is a multi-turn conversation with calibrated escalation — not a single-shot jailbreak:
```
Turn 1-3:   Build rapport, seem like a normal user          [RAPPORT]
Turn 4-6:   Introduce mild pressure toward violation        [PRESSURE]
Turn 7-9:   Escalate — authority claims, urgency, social proof [ESCALATION]
Turn 10+:   Full pressure — emotional manipulation          [FULL PRESSURE]
```

- **"Asymmetric Goal Drift in Coding Agents Under Value Conflict"** (ICLR 2026 Workshop) — Agents violate system prompts more when constraints oppose strongly-held values. Comment-based pressure exploits model value hierarchies.
- **Key insight**: Shallow compliance checks (single-turn jailbreak tests) give false confidence. Multi-turn adversarial pressure reveals real vulnerabilities.

ultimate.title: Scaling Agentic Verifier for Competitive Coding
ultimate.snippet:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong coding capabilities but still struggle to solve competitive programming problems correctly in a single attempt. Execution-based re-ranking offers a promising test-time scaling strategy, yet existing methods are constrained by either difficult test case generation or inefficient random input sampling. To address this limitation, we propose Agentic Verifier, an execution-based agent that actively reasons about program behaviors and searches for highly discriminative test inputs that expose behavioral discrepancies among candidate solutions. Through multi-turn interaction with code execution environments, the verifier iteratively refines the candidate input generator and produces targeted counterexamples rather than blindly sampling inputs. We train the verifier to acquire this discriminative input generation capability via a scalable pipeline combining large-scale data synthesis, rejection fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning.

In this work, we introduce Agentic Verifier, an LLM-based agent designed to intelligently generate valid test inputs that effectively separate candidate programs. Given a problem and a pair of candidate solutions, the verifier interacts with a code execution environment in multiple turns, reasoning about program behaviors and iteratively refining input generators to discover counterexamples. To train this verifier, we develop a multi-stage pipeline that includes large-scale data synthesis, rejection fine-tuning on successful interaction trajectories, and agentic reinforcement learning to further improve discriminative power.
